title: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
shortTitle: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
summary: Windows Credential Manager keeps saved sign-ins for websites, applications and network resources in containers called Credential Lockers, which older documentation described as Vaults. Entries for Internet Explorer and Edge live in the Web Credentials locker, while application and network entries sit in the Windows Credentials locker. Each locker is a folder of encrypted files inside the user profile, and the key that protects them is stored beside them, itself wrapped with the user's own logon material. Attackers therefore use the same store the operating system uses: the built-in vault command lists entries from a command line, the credential enumeration programming interface returns them to any process running as that user, and a copy of the folder can be decrypted offline once the wrapping key is unwrapped. Telemetry looks like command lines naming the vault utility, unusual processes loading vault libraries, or bulk reads of the locker directory. Help desk tools, remote support sessions and profile migrations legitimately touch the same paths, so capture the parent process and the account context before calling it malicious.

beginner.definition: The Windows Credential Manager is a built-in store for saved logins on a Windows computer. It holds website passwords and network or application credentials in protected folders called lockers. This technique means an attacker reads that store and steals the saved logins.
beginner.whyItMatters: Credential Manager often holds credentials for file shares, remote desktops, and internal services. Those are exactly the accounts an attacker needs in order to move sideways through a network. The store belongs to the signed-in user, so ordinary user rights are enough to read it. If you do not monitor this store, a quiet theft can look like normal user activity for weeks.
howItWorks: Windows saves the credentials you tick as remembered into containers called Credential Lockers.
Website entries go to the Web Credentials locker and network entries to the Windows Credentials locker.
The locker is a folder of encrypted files inside the user profile, one per saved credential.
A small policy file in the same folder holds the key, itself wrapped with your logon secrets.
An attacker runs the built-in vault command or calls a Windows interface to list entries.
They can also copy the whole folder and unlock it later once they hold the key material.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel front desk with a cabinet full of guest room keys. Staff keep the cabinet locked and hang its master key on a hook behind the desk. The system works well while everyone is honest, because guests only ask for their own key. Now a thief walks behind the desk wearing a staff shirt. The master key is right there, so they open the cabinet and copy every key inside it. Nothing was broken and no alarm rang. The thief used the same cabinet and the same key as the staff.
takeaways: Credential Manager is readable by the logged-in user, so user rights are enough to steal it.
Watch for the vault command or credential-listing interfaces started by unusual parent processes.
Remove saved network credentials that are not truly needed on user workstations.

objectives: Describe what a Credential Locker is and which kinds of credentials it holds.
Explain how the locker files are protected and where the key material is kept.
Recognise command lines and interfaces that enumerate credentials from the store.
Compare suspicious locker access with legitimate help desk and migration activity.
Suggest policy changes that reduce the number of saved network credentials.
